fields.title: Newly Desktop App
fields.description: One prompt bar, a live iPhone preview and a path to the App Store.
fields.intro: Newly is an AI agent that turns a conversation into a real iOS, Android or web app. As a contract design engineer and the only designer, I designed the desktop and web workspace and built parts of it in React and TypeScript.
fields.summary: I designed the workspace where people build apps with Newly’s agent, from the prompt bar to deploying to the App Store.
fields.overview: Newly is for technical and non-technical people alike. I worked with the founders and a team of six-plus, and changed course when feedback showed something wasn’t working.
fields.impact: Shipped on desktop and web, and helped grow Newly’s revenue.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.heading: How might we let anyone build and ship a real app with an AI agent, without losing track of what it’s doing?

children.text: Behind one text box sit local and cloud sessions, a simulator, git branches, model choices and releases to TestFlight and the App Store. That’s a lot to put in front of someone who has never written code, and a lot to keep in view for someone who has.
Who:
technical and non-technical people.
Where:
a desktop app and the web.
Constraint:
more ideas than time to build them.

Before any screen was final, there was a bigger question to answer: how should people actually work with Newly’s agent? You could manage your app like a project, with the agent proposing features you approve one at a time, or you could just talk to it and let the conversation lead. I explored a few directions before we picked one.

content.label: Ways to work with the agent

notes.text: A board where the agent proposes features you approve, build and deploy
A prompt bar above the board
Chat-first: just chat with the agent

children.text: My first direction treated your app like a roadmap. The agent proposed features as cards and explained its reasoning. You approved, built and deployed each one from a board.

content.alt: Early Newly workspace with a board of proposed features, the agent’s reasoning panel for one feature, and a live iPhone preview
content.caption: The board, with the agent’s reasoning open.

children.text: The board also made branching easy. Each feature card had a branch button, so you could split off a new idea with its own prompt. It worked a lot like a git worktree, but in a form non-technical people could understand more easily. Once a branch was accepted, it merged back into the card it came from.

content.alt: The Newly board with feature cards joined by lines: Dedicated Profile Tab is complete and ready to merge, and a New Idea card with its own prompt branches off Liquid Glass Styling
content.caption: A new idea branching off a card, next to one that’s ready to merge.

children.text: Another version put a prompt bar above the board.

content.caption: Board, then board with a prompt bar, then the chat-first direction that shipped.

images.alt: Newly home as a three-column board of proposed features
Newly home with a Welcome Back prompt bar above the feature board
The chat-first Newly workspace with sessions, conversation and a running iPhone simulator

children.text: Why we went with chat
People found the board slightly confusing.
They were more used to just chatting with an agent.
It was too much to build
in the time we had.
The founders and team chose chat-first,
and I designed the workspace around it.
The board never made it into production. I still think it’s a good picture of an agentic future, and it stays in the design files in case we come back to it.
Marketing, too

The agent was also meant to make marketing content for your app, like graphics and videos. I explored that on the board first, where media lived in a Marketing column and opened on the right with Publish and Download. The direction we went with is the chat: the agent shares the media in the conversation, and a switcher at the bottom of the preview panel flips between App and Images.

content.caption: Marketing content on the board, then in the chat, with a media switcher in the preview panel.

images.alt: The Newly board with a Marketing column of IG Slideshow and Video cards, and an IG Slideshow panel on the right with Publish, Download, four images and the agent’s reasoning
images.label: Board

images.alt: The Newly chat with the agent sharing an Instagram carousel, and the preview panel showing one of its images above an App and Images switcher
images.label: Chat

children.text: The sidebar is how you get around a project. It’s where you start a new session, search, deploy and configure your project, and your pinned and recent sessions are always one click away.

It sits on the left of the workspace. With chat chosen, the workspace became a set of panes you can open and collapse, with the chat in the middle and the preview panel on the right. I built this layout in code.
I call the right side the preview panel because it previews more than your app. It also shows the media the agent makes, and in the future, websites and code.

At first, app navigation and the session list were separate panes. Both could collapse, and the session list also acted like navigation. People found that a bit confusing, so we merged them into one sidebar.

content.caption: Two collapsible panes, then one sidebar.

images.alt: Earlier Newly layout with an app navigation pane (Create, Deploy, Analytics, Settings) next to a separate Sessions pane
images.label: Before

images.alt: Final Newly layout with one sidebar: New Session, Search, Deploy and Configure above pinned sessions and the session list, next to the chat and app preview
images.label: After

sections.title: Onboarding
sections.heading: From sign-up to the first prompt

children.text: Onboarding is the first few minutes anyone spends in Newly. It takes new users from signing up to their first prompt: a couple of quick questions about what they want to build, a short tour of how Newly works, and getting their Mac set up to build and run iOS apps.
A lot of it was designed and then prototyped in Claude Design before it shipped. The clips below are recorded from that prototype, so you can see its micro-interactions and animations.

content.caption: The welcome screen cycles through things you could make, then sign-up.

children.text: Two quick questions come next: what you want to build, and how much of this you’ve done before. Either one can be skipped. Then a three-card tour: say it once in plain English, change anything by asking, ship it to the App Store.

content.caption: What you’re building, how much you’ve done before, and the tour.

children.text: Local development needs Xcode and an iPhone simulator. Newly installs Xcode and boots the simulator for you, one step at a time, and shows each step as it runs. “Set this up later” skips straight to the workspace.

content.caption: Xcode and the simulator set up, then the workspace opens.

children.text: The start screen is where every new chat begins. It’s the place you come back to whenever you want to start something, whether that’s a brand new project or a new session in one you already have. From here you type your first prompt, choose where the session runs, use a shortcut or pick up where you left off. It didn’t always live in the main window, though.

Some earlier iterations started in a separate small window, like the startup windows in Xcode or Android Studio: your projects on one side, and Create New Project or Open Existing Project on the other.

content.caption: An earlier startup window, and the same window opening again over an open project.

images.alt: An early Newly startup window, Welcome to Newly, with a list of projects on the left and Create New Project and Open Existing Project on the right, floating on a blue wallpaper
images.label: On its own

images.alt: The same startup window opened again on top of the Newly workspace with a project already open
images.label: Over a project

children.text: We decided against it. We wanted everything in one window, and it was a bit confusing when the startup window opened again over a project that was already open.
In the final design, the start screen lives in the main window, and onboarding ends there. It works with or without a project open, and the biggest difference between the two is the sidebar:
No project open:
Home, Open Existing Project and Docs, then Projects (All Projects, Created by me, Shared with me) and Recents.
Inside a project:
the project, New Session, Search, Deploy and Configure, then pinned sessions and the session list.
A project organizer that opens from the sidebar is planned for the future.
The prompt bar is taller here than mid-chat, to draw your attention and make starting a chat feel balanced and important.
Below it there’s room for a stack of cards: a way back into a recent project, or an action worth promoting, like getting the mobile app.

content.caption: Two cards from the stack: “Pick up where you left off” outside a project, “Try the Newly Mobile App” inside one.

images.alt: Newly with no project open: a sidebar with Home, Open Existing Project, Docs, projects and recents, a tall prompt bar under Let’s make something new, and a Summer Project card to pick up where you left off
images.label: No project

images.alt: Newly inside the Travel App project: a sidebar with New Session, Search, Deploy, Configure, pinned sessions and sessions, a tall prompt bar under Hey Winston! Ready to build?, and a card to try the Newly mobile app
images.label: In a project

children.text: The prompt bar is how you talk to the agent. You describe what you want built or changed, attach files and images or record a voice message, pick a mode and send it off. While the agent works, the bar shows what’s happening and lets you stop it or line up your next message. It shows up all over the workspace, so it had to work at every size.
I built the prompt bar in React and TypeScript, mostly with Claude Code and Cursor. It changes with the space it has and what the agent is doing.
Modes people can find

In the old product, Build, Plan and Ask sat in a dropdown. PostHog showed people rarely used Plan or Ask, and some support requests asked for a mode that only answers questions without editing anything. That mode already existed. People just couldn’t find it.
So the modes moved into the bar as a segmented control, and only the active one shows its label:
It stays narrow
enough for every width.
It always says what will happen
when you send.
There’s less noise
next to what you’re typing.

content.alt: Three Newly prompt bars in Build, Plan and Ask mode, with only the active mode labelled
content.caption: Build, Plan and Ask. Only the active mode carries a label.

content.alt: The Newly prompt bar in expanded, stacked and collapsed layouts
content.caption: Expanded, stacked, collapsed.

children.text: Set once, at the start

A session can’t switch between remote and local once it starts. Only the model can change, and people rarely change it. So in a new session, location and model sit under the bar where you can’t miss them. Mid-chat, the model moves into the + menu, out of the way, especially for non-technical people.
Short copy in the menus
These menus had to give clear information without much text. Most options get a name and, at most, one short line:
Location
explains its trade-off: “Runs in the cloud, accessible on any device” or “Runs on your computer, device must stay awake”.
Models

say what you’re picking: Newly Agent is “Best all around”, and Codex and Claude each say “Uses your own subscription”. If you haven’t linked one yet, a small “+ LINK” next to it prompts you to link your own.
Effort
is a slider with one word for the current level, like “Medium”.

content.alt: Three popovers from the Newly prompt bar: Remote or Local session, Effort and Model, and the + menu with the model submenu
content.caption: The location menu, and the effort and model menu, at the start; the + menu mid-chat.

children.text: While the agent works
A
stop
button while it runs.
A
status line
while it connects or fixes a bug.
A
queue
, so you don’t lose your next thought. Runs can take minutes, and people wanted to line up their next change instead of waiting. Queued messages sit above the bar, where you can see and remove them.

content.alt: Eight states of the Newly prompt bar: drop files, attached images, audio message, stop, connecting, fixing bugs, and messages in queue
content.caption: Drop files, images, voice, stop, connecting, fixing bugs and the queue.

children.text: The conversation is where the agent talks back. It explains what it’s doing, shows the work behind each change, like the commands it ran and the code it wrote, and asks you questions when it needs a decision. Newly is for non-technical people too, so all of that had to stay easy to read without hiding anything. That starts with how the agent’s work is shown.
The agent’s work folds into one line, like “Worked for 3m, used 3 tools”.
Not everyone needs the commands.
Newly is for non-technical people too.
The chat stays readable
instead of turning into a log.
It’s still there to check.
Expanded, each step gets an icon, and code and commands sit in their own containers.

content.alt: The Newly chat panel on the blue wallpaper: the user’s message, the agent’s reply with its work folded into Worked for 3m, used 3 tools, and the prompt bar at the bottom
content.caption: The agent’s work, folded into one line, with the prompt bar below.

children.text: Prototyped in Claude Design

I used Claude Design to prototype the chat’s interactions and layouts, because I could simulate typing and chatting with the agent while I iterated on the designs. The four experiments below all shipped:
Markdown
in replies: headings, lists, inline code, tables and links.
Code and terminal
blocks: a live terminal, code with its filename, and diffs.
The tool list, expanded:
each tool with an icon and how long it took, and steps still running.
Questions in the prompt bar:
when the agent needs an answer, the bar turns into options to pick from.

content.alt: Four Newly chat experiments as selected frames on a dot grid: markdown in a reply, code and terminal blocks, the expanded tool list, and a question in the prompt bar
content.caption: The four chat experiments in Claude Design.

sections.title: Simulators panel
sections.heading: Controls that wait until you need them

children.text: The simulators panel is where you see your app actually running. It lives in the preview panel and runs your app on an iPhone simulator, in the cloud or on your computer, so you can try it out while the agent builds it. It comes with the controls you’d expect from a phone, like going home, rotating it or taking a screenshot, and a picker for choosing the device and iOS version.
There are a lot of those controls, but you don’t always need them. So they’re hidden. Two small dots on the side of the phone hint that there’s something there to hover.

content.caption: Two dots at rest. On hover, the backplate expands with the controls.

images.alt: The Newly preview panel with an iPhone simulator and two small dots beside the phone
images.label: Resting

images.alt: The same preview panel on hover: a backplate behind the phone has expanded, with a rail of controls on its right
images.label: On hover

children.text: On hover, the backplate under the phone expands, and a rail of controls appears on its right. Home sits in the centre, right where your mouse already is after hovering the dots. The top half holds controls for your app, like reloading it or taking a screenshot. The bottom half holds controls for the phone, like the app switcher and rotating it.

content.alt: The Newly workspace on a pale yellow-green wallpaper: the sidebar, a new chat, and the preview panel with the simulator’s backplate and control rail out
content.caption: The controls out, in the preview panel.

children.text: The panel works in landscape too.

content.alt: The Newly workspace with a landscape iPhone simulator in the preview panel, its backplate expanded and the control rail on the right
content.caption: In landscape, the rail stays on the right.

children.text: A clearer picker
The simulator picker went through eight versions. Tester feedback and my own critique pointed to two problems:
Unclear what was selected →
Cloud and Local got their own column, and the columns got labels: Type, Device, Version.
Unclear what Apply did →
it re-runs the app, so Apply became Apply & Run.

content.alt: Four versions of the iOS simulator picker, from a footer Cloud/Local toggle and an Apply button to labelled Type, Device and Version columns with Apply & Run
content.caption: Four of the eight versions.

children.text: Craft is about the visual details that run through the whole workspace: how the glass lets your wallpaper through, how corners and shadows are drawn, and where colour shows up. None of them are features on their own, but together they shape how Newly feels to use. Here’s where most of that polish went:
Glass.
I wanted your wallpaper to shine through the workspace nicely, so I played with different tinting methods until the blur tint felt right.
Corners
are concentric, so shapes inside each other feel like they belong together, and everything lines up. They’re also smoothed, which makes the whole thing feel more polished.
Shadows
are used lightly, just enough to give the important things a sense of depth.
Colour
is held back in the workspace. Blue only marks the active mode, the main action and anything running, so your own app stands out.
Together, it all feels crisp.

content.alt: Four close-ups of Newly: a smoothed corner, glass panes with the wallpaper coming through, a window over a blue wallpaper, and the Build, Plan and Ask control next to the send button, with nested corners and a soft shadow
content.caption: Smoothed corners, the wallpaper through the glass, and concentric corners with light shadows.

children.text: Deploy is where your app leaves Newly. Destinations are grouped by platform, so sending a build to TestFlight and the App Store, or publishing for Android and the web, happens in one place. Newly also runs in the browser, so you can get back to your projects without the desktop app. I designed and built the screens for both, and they’re live.
Deploy
groups destinations by platform. The App Store card shows a short checklist and the details already filled in.
The web app
opens with a “Pick up where you left off” card to reopen your last project.

content.caption: The Deploy hub, the App Store release card and the web welcome screen.

images.alt: The Newly Deploy hub with iOS, Android and Web destinations
The App Store release card with a checklist and an Automatically Completed list
Newly on the web: the welcome screen with a filled prompt and a Pick up where you left off card

sections.title: Outcome
sections.heading: What shipped and what I learned

children.text: The workspace, onboarding, the prompt bar and its states, the new chat features, the deploy flow and the web app are all live.
What feedback changed
Shaped by feedback:
chat over the board, one sidebar instead of two, and Apply & Run in the simulator picker.
After shipping:
people stopped getting stuck on the simulator picker.
What I learned
Designing for an agent is mostly states, not screens.
A good idea can still be wrong for the timeline. The board may come back.
Summary

One prompt in Newly drives sessions, a simulator, models and App Store releases, for technical and non-technical people. As the only designer, I designed the workspace around that prompt bar, from onboarding to the preview panel. I also built the layout, the prompt bar, and the deploy and web screens in React and TypeScript, and prototyped the chat and much of the onboarding in Claude Design.
Feedback and the team’s priorities changed the plan more than once along the way. What shipped helped grow Newly’s revenue.
